meta.title: Navigation
meta.description: The two buttons that move between shifts: what each one targets, what it is called, and what the count on it means.

basics.intro: Two buttons sit above and below the schedule, and they always move by one shift. Which shift that is depends on where the reader already is: the top button goes back to the start of the current shift while you are inside it, and only then to the shift before it.
basics.where: That rule is what makes the buttons predictable while reading: the first press never skips the shift you are in the middle of.

targets.intro: Written out, with A for the shift being read:
rows: Inside a later shift (A above the current one)
Inside the current shift, not at its start
The start of the current shift
At the start of the current shift
Inside an earlier shift, not at its start
At the start of the earliest rendered shift
Nothing: hidden in the list, disabled in the timeline
targets.count: When the top button points at an earlier shift, it also carries a count: how many items in the shifts already passed can still pin. That number is what tells a reader whether going back is worth it.

points: The visible label is the accessible name — no hidden name says something different from what the button shows.
The hint ("No previous shift available") is a tooltip and the button’s description, not its name.
In the list the buttons disappear when there is nowhere to go; in the timeline they stay, disabled, so the grid does not shift under the reader.
A jump is smooth unless the reader asked for reduced motion, and lands with the shift heading in view.
In the list the buttons appear only once some shift holds at least navigationThreshold items, so a short day is not cluttered by controls that do nothing.
localization.nav holds every label and hint, including the carried-over count.
renderNavLabel replaces what a button says; the navButton and carriedOverCount parts replace how it looks.
handlers.onNavigate can cancel a jump — for an unsaved change, for instance — and onNavigate reports the ones that happen.
list.navigationThreshold decides when the list shows the buttons at all.
Navigation moves within the rendered shifts only. Going beyond them is a date change, which your application performs.
There is no jump to an arbitrary shift: the buttons move one step at a time.
The buttons are part of the component and cannot be moved elsewhere on the page; a control of your own can call the same movements through the imperative handle.
